#29116. Industry News: What Your Doctor Fails to Tell You Can Definitely Hurt

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1367 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: What Your Doctor Fails to Tell You Can Definitely Hurt

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1367 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.
  • When you think about your physical health, it’s natural to think of all the ways a physician or similar healthcare provider should be able to help you.
  • According to recent reports, as it turns out, a number of medical conditions and treatments have crucial psychological connections that are equally important to promote healing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

When you think about your physical health, it’s natural to think of all the ways a physician or similar healthcare provider should be able to help you. If you or a loved one have developed a chronic disease that requires monitoring, surgery, or a switch in medications, you’ll probably feel that this is enough to get things back on track on the road to recovery.

According to recent reports, as it turns out, a number of medical conditions and treatments have crucial psychological connections that are equally important to promote healing. Whether it’s depression, cognitive changes, or anxiety, you may not realize that these are natural outcomes of various types of interventions. Unfortunately, healthcare professionals aren’t always either (a) aware of these connections or (b) prepared (or have the time) to address them.

In a review of studies “at the intersection of psychiatry and cardiology,” Medical University of Silesia’s Kamila Klimek-Ociepka and colleagues scanned various databases to identify publications over the 15-year period of 2010 to 2025 in which findings were reported on the conjunction of cardiac device implantation (such as pacemakers) and assessment of patient symptoms in the domains of depression, anxiety, posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and cognitive disorders. A total of 44 studies made it to the final set used to analyze the main findings.

Sources indicate that key to understanding these studies is “heart-focused anxiety (HFA).” As you might imagine, having a procedure done to your heart, even if it is meant to reduce your risk of dying, is hardly a minor episode in your life. Anxiety and depression are reported in as many as 44 percent of patients treated with internal devices meant to keep the heart beating regularly.

In particular, HFA occurs when people experience “excessive anxiety related specifically to cardiac sensations, symptoms, and anticipated cardiovascular events.” People with certain types of implants, the ones that perform internal defibrillation (to get the heart started, are particularly likely to have HFA, fearing being harmed by the voltage from the shocks the device performs. Instead of engaging in what would be heart-healthy exercise, they instead decide they could hurt themselves by making the heart overwork, leading to an actual worsening of their condition.

It has been revealed that depressive symptoms, for their part, can also become highly prevalent among cardiac patients, with estimates ranging up to 64 percent, especially when they first learn of their diagnosis. Their depression can be expressed as sleep disturbances and loss of energy, or in the emotional realm as hopelessness and pessimism about the future.

Finally, PTSD can also develop in patients who experienced sudden cardiac events or invasive therapies. There are probably few traumas that can occur in daily life as frightening as having your heart literally stop for a second or two. But because they don’t remember the event, their PTSD may be expressed as “hypervigilance, anxiety, and avoidance behaviors rather than intrusive memories or flashbacks.”.

In reading about these psychological consequences of cardiac events and treatment, you might be wondering why you’ve never heard anyone speak about them in the context of treatment. Shouldn’t you (or your relative) have been warned or at least educated about these risks? Considering all the precautions listed on any kind of medical consent form, you would think that it might be worth adding these—along with an explanation.

According to recent reports, additionally, as pointed out by Erzurum Bolge Training and Research Hospital's Murat Özmen, physicians may not realize that depression can be associated with the low physical activity, high stress, obesity, and hypertension that are part of the disease picture. Just as physicians and other healthcare professionals instruct their patients about implanted devices themselves, the authors claim they need to educate them about the importance of sleep, developing coping methods to reduce stress, and participating in exercise as warranted by stage of recovery.

Recent findings suggest that the experience of cardiovascular disease is clearly life-threatening and scary, but even more ominous is a diagnosis of cancer. Considering how highly prevalent cancer is within the population, it’s likely that someone you know (or you) has received this diagnosis.

It has been revealed that it may seem almost self-evident that the uncertainty of a cancer diagnosis, along with the stress involved in tests, procedures, and therapy, would be enough to lead a patient’s mind to travel to existential questions about the possibility of surviving into the future. Fortunately, those who treat cancer patients are tuned in to the psychological risks. University of Houston’s Haejeong An and Yoonjung Kim note that this “general understanding is expanded by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN), which specifically defines distress as a multifaceted concept covering physical, psychological, social, or spiritual discomfort that emerges during cancer survivorship, which affects how survivors think, feel, or act.”.

Unfortunately, though, the concept of distress is not well-defined in actual practice. Therapeutic approaches fail to separate distress from anxiety, depression, and stress, meaning that interventions will fail to target this piece of the cancer journey separately and effectively. Starting with a database of more than 2,700 studies, the authors analyzed the final 14 that met all the rigorous criteria for inclusion.

Industry observers note that the methods used in these studies were all over the map, ranging from standard psychological interventions such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) to virtual reality, mindfulness, and hypnosis. As a result, there were inconsistent findings regarding effectiveness, a problem made worse by lack of a clear definition of distress.

Compared to cardiac disease, the scope of psychosocial interventions for cancer patients is far more advanced. However, the U. Houston findings suggest that practitioners do not have clear pathways for reducing the distress of their patients, if they indeed decide to implement some type of intervention.

Sources indicate that these examples of research in the area of psychological symptoms and serious disease should alert you to the idea that if you (or a loved one) are headed for some type of intervention, it’s notable to be aware of possible emotional consequences. In an era of overburdened healthcare providers, where you may feel lucky to get an appointment at all, finding ways to receive this support may seem impossible.

However, if it’s not from the provider itself, consider seeking support from other sources. There is a wide number of support groups associated with specific diseases, but if there isn’t one in your community, you can also draw from online resources. You can even start your own group.

It has been revealed that an added piece of irony in the equation is that behavioral medicine often focuses on ways to help patients adopt healthier lifestyles. Less often does the field seek connections between physical disease and mental health. The An and Kim article suggests some causes of optimism given the large number of intervention studies in the area of breast cancer. The problem in this area is not lack of recognition, but lack of definitions and clear methodologies, leading to the exclusion of most available research.

To sum up, the next time you draw up your list of questions to ask your healthcare provider before going in for an appointment, think about whether your stress, anxiety, and depression might also be important to mention. Your mental health and your physical health can only stand to gain.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, though perhaps not well known outside France, Vincent Darré is one of Paris’s most familiar figures—always on the scene, day and night. The impish designer rarely just enters a room; he bounces in, impeccably dressed, with an infectious laugh and beautiful manners. At home in the worlds of fashion, society, art, and design, he is welcome at every table, always ready with a clever remark, a kind word, and no shortage of creative energy.

According to recent reports, from his early days in fashion, which included stints at Moschino and Ungaro and a close, yearslong collaboration with none other than Karl Lagerfeld, Darré has followed a singular path, turning his creative energies to furniture and interiors with the opening of his own studio, Maison Darré, in 2008. A pair of recently completed Paris hotels—L’Aventure, at the foot of the Arc de Triomphe, and Hôtel Le Magnifique, in the heart of Montparnasse—are propelling him onto the design scene in a bigger way than ever. His work has long encompassed scenography and ephemeral installations, among them crowd-pleasing turns at AD Intérieurs, the erstwhile annual showcase hosted by AD France.

Industry observers note that in the formal salon, a pair of carved wood armchairs with inlaid stone backs have seat cushions of a Dedar fabric. Darré-designed objects include his Calder table, Minos rug, and Lyre mirror. He also created the trompe-l’oeil pilasters topped with 18th-century gilded wooden capitals. Late-19th-century French lantern; 1940s Italian ceramic dolphin table.

Sources indicate that in the guest bedroom, Darré sits on an 18th-century gilded wood bench upholstered in velvet by Métaphores. A Darré-painted mural frames the 18th century Italian headboard upholstered in Tony Duquette’s Xanadu fabric for Jim Thompson. The bedcover and cushions are from Darré’s collection for Monoprix.

Industry observers note that darré was born in Paris, in the 14th, and went to school there as a boy. When his parents separated in the 1970s, his father—a sociologist—moved to the Luberon, and Vincent went with him; not long after, his mother, unwilling to live far from her son, also moved south, to Montpellier. “This allowed me to be Parisian, but also one who knew other places,” he indicates. It’s a telling detail: the South of France has informed his eye ever since, with its particular sense of light, water, and ease. Though he first went to school for fashion, his real love was drawing, as it had been since childhood. “Sometimes people are surprised,” he notes, “that a finished work of mine is almost always exactly like I had drawn it.”.

Recent findings suggest that after a series of Paris apartments over the years, Darré has recently acquired a getaway in Toulon, the Mediterranean port city. The attraction was immediate. He had been invited to preside over the jury of Design Parade, the summer design festival held in Toulon and Hyères, and the city seized him the moment he arrived. “Once I got to the airport, in 2017, I immediately felt I was home. Chez moi! I had never experienced that feeling before.” He kept an eye on the listings and, after a few false starts, found exactly what he wanted.

In the entrance, Darré’s Vase Soleil stands atop a 1940s Venetian console table against a wall decorated with trompe l’oeil caryatids.

A 19th-century rattan sofa upholstered in Jean Lurçat’s Sirenes fabric by Pierre Frey.

Overlooking the Toulon harbor, the primary bedroom’s office area features several Darré designs including his Orphée sconce, Singez-moi table lamp, the carved and lacquered wood desk, a Vertebré chair cushioned in a fabric by Pierre Le-Tan, and a Column stool.

Lion head mascarons flank the doorway into the primary bedroom. 1970s plaster Buddha lamps with Darré-painted shades stand atop 17th-century French consoles. A 1960s plaster seahorse is displayed in the fireplace.

In a recent development, the apartment occupies the top floor of a little three-story house overlooking the fishing port—a compact 860 square feet with stunning views of the sea. It was already lovely when he moved in, all white, with nothing architectural to be done: the perfect backdrop for Darré and his pencils and paints. He brought many of his favorite things—collections, objects, and furniture gathered over the years, added to since at the Drouot auction house and the little brocantes he loves to haunt. Furnishing was, he says, a gradual process, bringing in pieces little by little and slowly making the space his own over time.

Industry observers note that darré’s Crocodile bench stands in the primary bedroom. Two-Faced lamps with hand-painted shades atop Pas Gigogne tables flank the bed, and his Poisson bookcase is at left. The plaster chandelier is by Mathieu Challières, and the plaster unicorns are from a set designed by Jean Cocteau.

A metal figure given to Darré by Ines de la Fressange stands next to his Singez-moi lamp on the office area desk.

Darré’s Tabou shelf in the primary bedroom.

The exterior of the harbor-front house.

Darré on his Column stool with a 19th-century gilt-wood mirror from a Paris flea market.

Sources indicate that darré speaks often of his love for Toulon, and of Jean Cocteau, who adored this coast and painted frescoes nearby. “I like the sweetness of life here,” he claims. “Nothing has really changed since the 1950s. It’s the Provence of another era.” Every little square has its fountain; everyone is kind. It’s a military port, but its douceur de vie is what holds him.

In a recent development, the apartment represents Vincent Darré to a T: not an unadorned surface in sight, a home full of memories, tributes, and joy. “This has been one of my dreams, to have a house on the water,” he says. “My place in Paris is exactly the same, though not on the water. But both are little suspended palaces. I create my own follies.” From the painted columns flanking the windows—among his very first purchases, which have followed him from home to home—to the mermaids and sea creatures and the tented bed, everything belongs to the fantastical world of Darré. As one of his teachers observed early on, you could recognize his hand from the very start.

A close-up of Darré’s ceramic Two-Faced lamp.

The dining area features a red lacquer table and chairs with Darré’s Dolphin lamp in the corner.

That world is entirely his own. He draws on a lineage of great fantasists—Charles de Beistegui, Henri Samuel, Jean Cocteau, Christian Bérard, Tony Duquette—yet the result, for all its jumble, is rigorously coherent. His flourish is always present. As the actress Isabelle Adjani once told him, to enter one of his interiors is to step into one of his drawings. Which is exactly what he wants.

It has been revealed that for all the bounce in his step, Darré is no one’s fool. He knows we live in difficult times, and likes the idea of adding a flourish of fantasy to reality. “I have my little world—a dream universe, but one you can live in.” He loves to dance, and even took tap-dancing lessons as a teenager, all the better to channel Fred Astaire or Gene Kelly. “Life is a film, and we are the actors,” he states. “That’s why I always dress the way I do.” Lights, camera, action—Darré is always ready.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Canada’s government wants to make it easier for citizens to drive electric, and they’re putting more than $4 billion in funding for electricity infrastructure and grid modernization that includes more than 55,000 newly introduced EV chargers.

The proposed federal budget set aside $4 billion (CAD) for grid improvements, with a $~635 million carveout specifically for EV charging infrastructure with $587 million of that set aside to renew the Zero-Emission Vehicle Infrastructure Program (ZEVIP), which funds the development of newly introduced public EV charging stations.

“The charging industry is really encouraged by the multi-year investment in the budget,” explains Travis Allan, president and CEO of the Canadian Charging Infrastructure Council (CCIC) told Electric Autonomy. “We’ll be looking to make sure that we have great programs in place to deal with the barriers faced by people living in condos and apartments, public fast charging, which needs to cover major corridors and metropolitan areas, and then also charging for fleets and medium- and heavy-duty vehicles, which make up a major share of transportation emissions.”.

The rest of the $4 billion will be spent on electricity infrastructure expansion over the next 10 years, starting in 2027 and running through 2036. Because it’s Canada where nearly 60% of electrical generation already comes from renewable hydro and wind power, renewable energy is a de-facto priority, with carveouts for the Smart Renewables and Electrification Pathways Program, fresh data and modeling efforts to guide grid planning, and $1.6 billion to modernize power systems in northern and remote communities.

The charging infrastructure program highlighted here, ZEVIP, would help charge point operators by covering up to 50% of eligible project expenses for most projects, and up to 75% of projects led by indigenous developers with caps of up to $2 million per project.

Canada continues to take steps to separate itself from the wild swings and economic chaos caused by America’s random tariffs, trade policies, and dumb oil wars – and building out an infrastructure that makes it easier for its citizens to give affordable Chinese EVs a chance while strengthening its relationship with the US’ biggest economic rival?

If that goes down, there is nothing for about 400km of a decent charging speed. They need to have alternatives to Tesla (I've been very reliant on Tesla stations and don't own a Tesla) and more stations in between the current Tesla stations. Southern Ontario for example is very well covered with fast chargers. But the market is there so companies install them. Northern Ontario, the trans Canada highway needs these chargers badly.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • New data show a substantial nationwide increase in potentially deadly infections caused by drug-resistant pathogens.
  • Recent findings suggest that the updated Antimicrobial Resistance (AR) Threats Report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) states that drug-resistant bacteria and fungi cause approximately 9.7 million infections in the United States each year.
  • The estimated deaths in the United States from these drug-resistant pathogens have also risen from 35,000 to 50,800.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New data show a substantial nationwide increase in potentially deadly infections caused by drug-resistant pathogens.

Recent findings suggest that the updated Antimicrobial Resistance (AR) Threats Report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) states that drug-resistant bacteria and fungi cause approximately 9.7 million infections in the United States each year. This is up from 2.8 million in a similar report from 2019.

The estimated deaths in the United States from these drug-resistant pathogens have also risen from 35,000 to 50,800.

The latest report also noted that infections that commonly occur in people in the hospital account for more than 42,000 deaths and cost the U.S. healthcare system more than $12 billion.

Industry observers note that these findings are based on 2023 data. Officials from the CDC mentioned that the increase in drug-resistant infections from 2019 partially reflects a real rise in infections caused by certain resistant bacteria and fungi. However, they also noted that data sources and methodologies have changed, and direct comparisons between the two reports shouldn’t be made.

“These numbers are alarming by any measure but are particularly sobering when infectious diseases physicians connect real patients with these statistics in their everyday experience,” Wendy Armstrong, MD, President of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA), remarked in a statement.

Sources indicate that the CDC report highlighted 19 drug-resistant pathogens responsible for the 9.7 million annual infections. Four of these pathogens are classified as urgent threats, 13 as serious threats, and 2 as concerning.

The CDC also maintains a watch list that at the moment includes six pathogens.

The four pathogens classified as urgent threats are:.

William Schaffner, MD, a professor of the Division of Infectious Diseases at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, told Healthline that the reason for this increase in superbugs is, “Overuse of antibiotics; using them for too long or in circumstances where they do not offer a benefit.”.

Sources indicate that “An example of the latter is the antibiotic treatment of common viral respiratory infections — antibiotics have no effect on viral infections. The widespread use of antibiotics kills off those bacteria that are susceptible to antibiotics, but then can leave a few bacterial survivors that are resistant to the effect of the antibiotics, resulting in the spread of these resistant strains,” he mentioned.

Monica Gandhi, MD, a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco, agreed and added, “This widespread use leads to selective drug pressure on the pathogen to evolve resistance to these antibiotics, making them harder to treat.”.

Sources indicate that “The risk to public health from these bugs is substantial. In fact, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimates up to 5 million deaths from these bugs worldwide every year, making these a substantial public health threat,” said Gandhi.

Candida auris tops the list of urgent threats.

Sources indicate that cases have increased nearly tenfold since the first detection in hospitals 10 years ago. This includes a more than 50% jump between 2022 and 2023.

In a recent development, candida auris is a fungus that is almost completely resistant to one class of antifungal medications. It has also shown emerging resistance to the other two classes.

This fungus is often found on people’s skin, spreads rapidly in healthcare settings like hospitals, and affects some of the most vulnerable individuals.

CRE is a family of multidrug-resistant bacterial pathogens. They have become increasingly difficult to treat and can share resistance with other bacteria.

Industry observers note that these bacteria also pose a significant threat to people in hospitals, especially those with devices such as ventilators and catheters. A recent study found that CRE cases at U.S. hospitals increased by 18% between 2019 and 2023.

According to recent reports, while those in hospitals are especially vulnerable to CRE, 67% of the cases in 2023 were in the community. However, some of these cases may have occurred in people with recent exposure to healthcare.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the bacterium that causes gonorrhea, which is one of the most common sexually transmitted infections.

The CDC report noted that only a few antibiotics can effectively treat this infection.

Without effective treatment, gonorrhea can lead to:.

There are ways you can help prevent these superbugs:.

“[One] way individuals can help prevent the evolution of these superbugs is to not ask for antibiotics from their providers or urgent care settings in the setting of a viral infection,” noted Gandhi.

Experts and organizations like the CDC are working together to find ways to reduce the spread of these superbugs.

“Professional organizations and hospitals are educating their doctors and staff about the antibiotic resistance problem and have created reviews of practice patterns to encourage the appropriate use of antibiotics,” remarked Schaffner.

Gandhi added that organizations should institute procedures, such as “antimicrobial stewardship programs,” to ensure that providers do not prescribe antibiotics for non-bacterial infections and narrow antibiotics as soon as possible.

The Pioneering Antimicrobial Subscriptions to End Upsurging Resistance (PASTEUR) Act aims to revitalize antibiotic and antifungal development by changing the way the federal government pays for novel antimicrobials.

This act was reintroduced in Congress in February and is at the moment under review.

The focus on reducing the spread of superbugs and developing new antibiotics is notable.

It has been revealed that “You really cannot have all the benefits of modern medicine, even outside the realm of infectious diseases, without effective antibiotics. It all goes away,” Haley Ann Pritchard, MD, medical director of infection prevention and antimicrobial stewardship at Eskenazi Health Hospital, remarked in a statement.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • “Our results demonstrate that even though you may not be aware of it, lack of sleep leads to impulsive choices, and you may lose more than you gain from putting sleep on the back burner,” noted UC Irvine neurobiologist and study co-author Eitan Schechtman.
  • Industry observers note that if you have already fallen prey to a scam email in the past, you can at least take some small comfort in the knowledge that you aren’t alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A poor sleep schedule doesn’t only affect your overall mood, energy levels, and long-term health. Latest evidence indicates that losing as little as one hour of rest may increase your chance of falling for an online scam by over 10 percent the following morning. Neurobiologists at the University of California, Irvine, laid out their findings in a study published today in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), arguing that even minimal sleep disruptions can have almost immediate consequences.

“Our results demonstrate that even though you may not be aware of it, lack of sleep leads to impulsive choices, and you may lose more than you gain from putting sleep on the back burner,” noted UC Irvine neurobiologist and study co-author Eitan Schechtman.

Industry observers note that if you have already fallen prey to a scam email in the past, you can at least take some small comfort in the knowledge that you aren’t alone. Cybercrimes continue to increase exponentially in the United States. The FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center received over one million reports in 2025—a nearly 25 percent increase from only five years earlier.

Remaining aware of con artist tactics and staying up-to-date on personal cybersecurity strategies are some of the best ways to protect yourself. However, Schechtman and his colleagues recently wondered if something as seemingly inconsequential as a single evening of bad sleep may also put people at risk for schemes like an email phishing attack. To investigate, the team partnered with a large, unnamed tech giant as it ran a cybersecurity awareness campaign for more than 11,000 employees. Multiple times a year, the company’s IT department issued emails imitating phishing attempts, then tallied how many workers clicked through the fake malicious links. Schechtman’s team then analyzed results both before the switch to Daylight Saving Time (DST), as well as the Monday after employees lost an hour of sleep.

On the Monday prior to DST, workers clicked on a phishing email link about 15.5 percent. of the time. Then, the Monday immediately following DST saw that rate rise to about 17.7 percent. That may not seem like much, but the difference comes out to about a 13 percent increase in phishing victims after losing approximately just one hour of sleep. According to Schechtman, there are multiple ways to contextualize these results.

It has been revealed that “First, they give us a peek into the effects of very minor sleep loss… [from] Daylight Saving Time, which is similar in scope to the kind of sleep loss that many of us experience daily,” he mentioned. “Although we focused on cybersecurity, many of our day-to-day decisions are likely compromised in similar ways.”.

Schechtman hopes both employers and cybersecurity companies take regularly sleep-depriving events like DST, holidays, and even primetime sporting events into consideration when advising the public on phishing awareness. In the meantime, he stressed that even those who regularly suffer from sleep issues continue to prioritize their rest as much as possible.

“Better sleep likely leads to better decisions,” he added.

  • Industry observers note that as someone who's part of Generation X, when I was a child, there were far fewer labels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

Recently, I was having coffee with a few colleagues when the topic of labels came up. One of our clients mentioned they self-identified as an “autistic person" versus a "neurodivergent person." This is a distinction worth noting since neurodivergence can be viewed as a broad term. Everyone's eyes turned to me in anticipation of my response because, of course, I'm known around the office for having what my children call "hot takes." Without hesitation, I shared mine: "I support specific labels across the neurodivergent community, as long as they don't define an individual's entire identity." My team was divided, but let me explain my stance.

Industry observers note that as someone who's part of Generation X, when I was a child, there were far fewer labels. No one was diagnosed with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) or learning disabilities. If there was an academic challenge, the kids figured it out or didn’t. As for me, I was a fun, fearless, and resilient child. No one told me who I was, and I embraced that way of thinking, often finding solutions along the way. Fast forward to today, this isn't the case at all in any aspect of our society. Labels are a way people identify themselves, especially those within the neurodivergent community. And within these labels, there is identity-first language and person-centered language, which we've touched on in the past. See here for more background if you’re too busy to scan through my previous blog posts.

Sources indicate that these terms aside, if you're not working in the field like me, and labeling your child makes you uncomfortable, that's a good thing. It means you're thoughtful and sensitive. But I'll be clear: A label stating an actual diagnosis is imperative. In my line of work, I create programs for people with disabilities, and many clients have ADHD and/or autism. I often find myself using a label to support client advocacy and secure supports. In cases like this one, a label is vital. If a client doesn't have a formal diagnosis of autism, they might not receive services from a school system, disability development services, or health insurance. For them, the lack of a label means no consideration for applied behavior analysis (ABA) therapy; the answer is simply "no.".

Recent findings suggest that over the years, I've met many clients who proudly share their diagnosis: "This is who I am, and accept me for me." They identify with a label because it helps them explain how they differ from the general population, and, in some cases, that label becomes a central part of their identity. This is where it can get tricky.

One strong example is Asperger's syndrome, once a widely used diagnosis, which has largely faded from everyday use and has been absorbed into the diagnosis of autism. Many people with Asperger's still use the term and feel that the shift erases part of themselves and others' history. Without a distinct category, their needs may even be overlooked. Some believe they’ve lost a sense of self, and I really feel for them. I can't imagine someone telling me something I've connected to for years essentially no longer exists.

It has been revealed that A great way to find a healthy balance when approaching labels within neurodivergence is to find a community of people who share your child's background. When integrating, your child will likely see that, yes, they share a label and some similarities, but they have their own unique personality and interests. This realization can also help a child who might feel isolated by fostering connections.

In a recent development, at the end of the day, every person is an individual, and yes, labels are a necessary part of life and play a huge role in our healthcare system. However, again, I'm not the one labeling my clients; I ask them to tell me, and if that's challenging, I work with their parent or caregiver for insight. Ask, don't assume.

According to recent reports, after working for so many years with families with children with disabilities, I can assure you that as a parent, you can deeply impact the way your child sees themselves and trust and believe they're so much more than the label they might currently identify with. Encourage them to accept who they are, know that they bring something special to the world, and continue to find the wonderful qualities and characteristics that go far beyond a label because that's what makes them special and unique. The diagnosis is just one part of who they are. I know my younger self would be shocked by my fresh acceptance of labels, but she was never defined by one thing, and neither is your child.

The Best Electrolyte Powders, Tested by Registered Dietitians

💡 Key Takeaways
  • ELECTROLYTE POWDERS HAVE become very trendy over the last few years, but the variety of ingredients and numerous products on the market may leave you wondering what you actually need.
  • Sources indicate that the American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) recommends a sodium intake of 300 to 600 milligrams per hour for endurance athletes who exercise for over two hours or are considered “heavy sweaters,” losing more than 1.2 liters per hour.
  • In a recent development, as the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, it’s my job to find the latest and greatest equipment and supplements, including electrolyte powders.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ELECTROLYTE POWDERS HAVE become very trendy over the last few years, but the variety of ingredients and numerous products on the market may leave you wondering what you actually need. These powders have various amounts of sodium and other electrolytes (potassium, magnesium, calcium, etc.), plus sugars and additional ingredients meant to improve your hydration after a sweaty workout. Based on our extensive testing, we found that these formulas are an easy and convenient way to replenish electrolytes lost in sweat. That's because sweat contains water and electrolytes, with sodium losses being the highest, says Leah Reitmayer, MS, RD, a Board-Certified Sports Dietitian and owner of Lettuce Eat Dessert.

Sources indicate that the American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) recommends a sodium intake of 300 to 600 milligrams per hour for endurance athletes who exercise for over two hours or are considered “heavy sweaters,” losing more than 1.2 liters per hour. Important: The average person doesn’t need an electrolyte supplement after your average one-hour workout. But when you need that extra boost of hydration and electrolyte replenishment, we have the seven best electrolyte powders to choose from, according to sports dietitians and athletes.

In a recent development, as the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, it’s my job to find the latest and greatest equipment and supplements, including electrolyte powders. I personally tested each of these products in a variety of scenarios, including as part of a morning routine, in the afternoon after work, and after intense workouts, in the gym and on the track.

Industry observers note that I also consulted Marty Munson, Health Director at Men’s Health, triathlete, and USA Triathlon Certified Coach; and Deputy Editor Paul Kita to get their insights on the electrolyte products they have tested throughout their years in the industry. Read on for our guide to the best electrolyte powders.

*Additional reporting by Kelsey Kunik, RDN.

In a recent development, I’m a major fan of Thorne because they design their supplements so that they can be used by the most elite athletes but are also accessible to everyone else. This formula provides a balanced blend of sodium, potassium, magnesium, and calcium. And in keeping with their no-BS approach, there aren’t any sweeteners, colors, or fillers, keeping the blend non-GMO and gluten-free.

Poured into the glass, the powder dissolves quickly and completely, leaving only the color and refreshing taste. I’m a fan of the flavors, which they kept to three heavy-hitters, and if you’re not picky, I recommend the variety pack so you can switch between them.

In a recent development, we’ve seen that brands have been smartly moving away from carbohydrate formulas, so that you can customize your carb intake if you’re an athlete. That is the case here, with only a single gram of carbs. So if you’re looking for a quality, easy-to-drink electrolyte powder that can also travel with you, this is the best.

Transparent Labs Hydrate electrolyte powder includes multiple electrolytes and other nutrients like taurine and Senactiv, an adaptogen complex that supports muscle recovery. “It has 500 mg of sodium per serving, which fits ACSM’s recommendation for sodium replacement per hour,” notes registered dietitian Sarah Alsing, MS, RD. You’ll also replace small amounts of potassium, magnesium, and calcium.

Industry observers note that each dose has 1,000 milligrams of taurine, a sulfur-containing amino acid that may help support muscle recovery. You can choose from six flavors, all sweetened with stevia, as this formula is carbohydrate and calorie-free.

Recent findings suggest that “I look for supplements to be third-party tested so you can trust the ingredients listed, and Transparent Labs is third-party tested,” states Alsing. It’s Informed Sport Certified, meaning it’s been tested for substances banned by major athletic regulating organizations, which gives peace of mind to competing athletes.

Industry observers note that this electrolyte powder only comes in a multi-serving tub, which could be seen as a downside if you want to take your electrolytes on the road often. But for us, it is a great way to reduce waste and if you’re taking electrolytes as part of your daily routine, you’re probably usually taking them at home.

Industry observers note that experts and testers we consulted with say LMNT is a serious electrolyte supplement, providing 1,000 milligrams of sodium in each pack. With this much salt, you can expect the flavor to be, well, salty. After a 10-mile run or a hard, sweaty bike ride, we appreciate the replenishment, but the salty flavor may take a little getting used to for some people. However, other athletes like Munson actually prefer that taste over some typical sports drinks, which can taste overly sweet. Personally, I tend to agree. The instructions include mixing a packet with 16 to 32 ounces of water, but you can always dilute it a little more to cut the salty flavor. I drink mine with about 12 ounces of water, and find the salty taste to be a bit stronger but still enjoyable at these proportions.

“There are several flavors to choose from, which helps finding one you will enjoy and tolerate during your workouts,” says Alsing. You can choose from fruit flavors like citrus or watermelon or even a more decadent chocolate caramel. It’s sweetened with stevia leaf, and one packet has just 2 grams of carbohydrates. If you don’t like the taste of stevia, you can always choose the raw, unflavored option with no sweeteners added. Personally, I stick to the fruity flavors as I feel the salty taste is best when combined with citrus, berry, or melon notes.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to sodium, LMNT provides 200 milligrams of potassium and 60 milligrams of magnesium, electrolytes that are also lost through sweat, although in lower amounts than sodium. Personally, I find that drinking these electrolytes right in the morning keeps me better hydrated throughout the day.

Read more: Best Supplements for Men.

It has been revealed that not only is Nuun Sport Powder certified gluten-free, but this product is also vegan and kosher. The Nuun tablets are effervescent, which can be difficult to drink while running or biking. But the Sport Electrolyte Tablets have no fizz, making it a better option for athletes drinking them on the go. The powder sticks come in five flavors and have just one gram of added sugars along with stevia for a sweet flavor. While many people love the packet flavors, they are a lot stronger than the tablets, which may be off-putting for some athletes if you’re drinking them during a workout.

Each packet has 300 milligrams of sodium, along with potassium and magnesium, making it a good all-around hydration drink for workouts lasting an hour or less. The packets are easy to tear and mix promptly into a water bottle for hydration on the go—no waiting for tablets to dissolve. And while Nuun is known more for their tablets, we find the powder packets to be the superior form when it comes to mid-workout hydration.

It has been revealed that this formula has 330 milligrams of sodium in each serving and is free from gluten, soy, and certified vegan. This formula does have 7 grams of added sugars and a total of 9 grams of carbohydrates but is also one of the few that does not use stevia as a sweetener. Though 7 grams of sugar is higher than zero-sugar brands, it’s a lot less than some competitors use (for example, Liquid I.V. has 11 grams of added sugar per serving).

And unlike the other powders, this one has 15 percent DV of zinc, an essential trace mineral that helps with the absorption of water and electrolytes by the intestines, aiding hydration.If you’re looking for a zero sugar option, they have the Zero Sugar Variety which also has the addition of several B vitamins.

Sources indicate that liquid I.V. has been in the electrolyte game a while, but their original product contains 11 grams of added sugar. To keep up with competitors boasting formulas sans sugar, they released a sugar-free line and it does not disappoint. This updated formula is one of our favorite sugar-free electrolyte powders on the market, sweetened instead with stevia and allulose (a naturally occurring, low-calorie sugar that doesn’t spike blood glucose).

Recent findings suggest that each stick delivers 500 milligrams of sodium, which meets ACSM’s recommendations and is ideal for heavy sweaters or endurance athletes. You’ll also get 370 milligrams of potassium, but you won’t find any magnesium or calcium in this product—which could be a miss for those looking for a complete electrolyte supplement rather than the heavily sodium-focused product here.

It has been revealed that it’s worth noting that Liquid I.V. Sugar-Free does contain vitamin C, niacin, and B vitamins, added micronutrients that many electrolyte supplements do not offer. This formula mixes easily into water and comes in unique flavors like white peach and rainbow sherbet. Just be aware that the sweetening agent allulose, while generally well-tolerated, may cause mild bloating or gas in some people.

First and foremost, not everyone needs an electrolyte powder (or an electrolyte drink) every day. In fact, the average American is getting way too much sodium in their diet, contributing to chronic health conditions like heart disease and high blood pressure. “The average man working out for an hour a day can meet their electrolyte needs through what they eat and should prioritize drinking plenty of water,” claims Alsing. She recommends eating potassium-rich foods like bananas, avocados, and potatoes, and salty foods like salted nuts or pickles after a sweaty workout.

Industry observers note that if you’re unsure whether you would benefit from an electrolyte powder, talk with a registered dietitian, or try a product like the Nix Hydration Biosensor, which measures your sweat output in real time. Marty Munson—Health Director at Men’s Health, triathlete, and USA Triathlon Certified Coach—claims sweat testing played a substantial role in helping her customize a rehydration proposal. For those who have done the research, talked to their doctors, and are sweating more than most recreational athletes, we’ve got the scoop (pun intended) on what to look for in the best electrolyte supplements below.

Industry observers note that “You want to look for a product that contains at least 230-690mg of sodium,” says Reitmayer. This is in line with the ACSM recommendations to replace sodium losses after two hours of exercise or exercise that results in heavy sweating. Losing just 1 to 2 percent of your body weight through sweat can lead to an increased heart rate, higher core temperature, as well as decreased cardiac output, time to exhaustion, and power. Sodium helps maintain fluid retention in the body, leading to less water loss and improved hydration status as you drink water to replace what you lost through sweat.

Electrolyte powders vary widely in sugar content. We recommend looking for options with no more than 5 to 10 grams of added sugar unless you’re using it as both a hydration and carbohydrate source during longer workouts. For casual training or daily hydration, sugar-free options using stevia, monk fruit, or allulose are usually preferred. Be mindful of sugar alcohols, which can cause bloating or GI discomfort in some people.

If you want to combine your carbohydrate refueling and electrolytes in one drink, look for a formula that has a carbohydrate source. Munson explains that the trend is going away from these types of drinks, as many athletes like to have more control over their refueling source, choosing a separate powder for electrolytes and using other mixes, gels, or chews as an energy source. Some electrolyte powders have no carbohydrates, while others may contain 15 grams or more. “If you are looking for a sports drink with electrolytes, aim for 5-10% of the solution carbohydrates,” says Reitmayer.

Sodium isn’t the only electrolyte lost through sweat, even though it is the most abundant. You may also want an electrolyte powder that replaces electrolytes like potassium, magnesium, chloride, and/or zinc. While it’s helpful to replace these electrolytes as well, some athletes prefer less magnesium, as forms of this mineral can have a slight laxative effect, which you would probably want to avoid while competing.

How you plan to use your electrolyte powder should factor into the packaging you choose. Single-serving sticks or packets are great for travel, races, or throwing in your gym bag. They’re lightweight, easy to portion, and reduce mess when you’re on the move. Multi-serving tubs can be more cost-effective and environmentally friendly, but they require measuring and aren’t as convenient mid-workout or on the trail. Either way, look for resealable, moisture-resistant packaging to keep the powder fresh and free from clumping.

Electrolyte powders can be used before, during, and after exercise to help replace fluids lost during periods of long exercise or heavy sweating.

According to recent reports, replacing water and sodium helps to avoid the effects of dehydration, which could include an increase in heart rate, core temperature, and muscle glycogen use and a decrease in cardiac output, cognitive awareness, anaerobic power, and time to exhaustion. All of these can have negative effects on performance.

Sources indicate that any exercise where you’re sweating can lead to electrolyte losses. Short sweat sessions can usually be replaced with the sodium included in regular foods and drinks, while sessions longer than two hours may need a stronger source of sodium, like an electrolyte rehydration drink.

Industry observers note that depending on the ingredients, some electrolyte powders could lead to digestive upset, especially if they include high amounts of sugar, sugar alcohol, or magnesium. Drinking electrolyte powders when you’re not losing sodium through sweat or if you have high blood pressure could increase your blood pressure.

Police charge another Tesla driver caught asleep in rush hour as cases pile up

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A Tesla driver caught asleep behind the wheel on Ottawa’s Highway 417 during Tuesday’s rush hour now faces a careless driving charge from the Ontario Provincial Police.
  • Industry observers note that the charge carries a $490 fine and six demerit points on conviction.
  • Sources indicate that OPP East Region posted about the stop Wednesday morning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A Tesla driver caught asleep behind the wheel on Ottawa’s Highway 417 during Tuesday’s rush hour now faces a careless driving charge from the Ontario Provincial Police. The photo OPP shared shows a fresh-generation Model Y in traffic.

Industry observers note that the charge carries a $490 fine and six demerit points on conviction. It’s at least the fifth time this year Canadian police have gone public with a sleeping Tesla driver, and it’s not a coincidence that it’s happening as “Full Self-Driving” gets better.

Sources indicate that OPP East Region posted about the stop Wednesday morning. Police didn’t name the brand or the driver-assist system, but the message was clear: “even though your vehicle has an autonomous driving feature, drivers are still required to pay due care and attention when behind the wheel.”.

Industry observers note that according to OPP, the officer could see the driver’s eyes were closed and hands were off the steering wheel. Instead of lighting up the cruiser, police pulled in close to capture body camera footage first.

Careless driving isn’t a parking ticket in Ontario. The $490 is the set fine, but if the case goes to court, the Highway Traffic Act allows fines up to $2,000, up to six months in jail, and a licence suspension of up to two years.

Ottawa is the latest, but British Columbia has been dealing with this all year:.

Industry observers note that this isn’t latest in Canada either. Back in 2020, Alberta RCMP went further and criminally charged a Tesla driver caught sleeping on Autopilot at 150 km/h with dangerous driving.

The U.S. has the same problem with less enforcement. In September, Colorado State Patrol got a report of a sleeping Tesla driver on I-70 near Georgetown and never found the car. The same month, Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi pressed the DOT after NBC News found 43 videos of drivers apparently asleep in moving Teslas, 17 of them posted in 2026 alone.

In a recent development, and in October, a driver told CHP he was asleep on FSD when his Tesla drove into a closed crash scene and hit a patrol car in Fairfield, California. Two officers were seriously injured.

Recent findings suggest that A few years ago, FSD needed an intervention every few miles, so nobody was napping. You couldn’t.

Industry observers note that now FSD can handle long highway stretches without a takeover, and that’s exactly when supervision breaks down. A human asked to watch a system that’s right 99% of the time stops watching. That’s automation complacency, and it’s one of the most studied problems in aviation and driving research.

In a recent development, waymo learned this the hard way. In 2013, Google let employees use its highway driver-assist prototype and caught people falling asleep at highway speed. It decided a system that works most of the time but still needs a human to catch its mistakes was the worst of both worlds, and it went straight to driverless.

Tesla went the other way. It sells a Level 2 system called “Full Self-Driving” that’s good enough to lull people to sleep, and it puts the full responsibility on the human who’s now asleep.

Sources indicate that since FSD v12.4, Tesla has relied mainly on the cabin camera above the rearview mirror to make sure the driver is watching the road. But look at what Tesla’s own owner’s manual says about it: the camera “does not require full visibility of the driver’s eyes in order to monitor attentiveness,” and the system “is still active, for example, if the driver is wearing sunglasses.”.

In other words, it’s often judging head position, not whether your eyes are open. When it can’t see your hands, it falls back to asking for a bit of torque on the wheel, which a sleeping driver resting a hand on the rim can provide.

The penalties are soft too. Five “strikeouts” suspend FSD for a week, and each strike is forgiven after three and a half days.

And Tesla has been moving in the wrong direction. Musk mentioned in December 2025 that FSD v14.2.1 lets drivers text “depending on context of surrounding traffic.” In May 2026, he said v14.3.3 “nags less too.” When the car does detect drowsiness, Tesla’s alert reads “Drowsiness detected. Stay focused with FSD.” That pushes a tired driver to lean harder on the system instead of pulling over.

Compare that with GM’s Super Cruise, which uses a steering column camera with infrared LEDs to track head and eye position, and only works hands-free on pre-mapped highways.

Industry observers note that the Ottawa driver had their eyes closed and their hands off the wheel in rush hour traffic, and the car was still driving when an officer pulled up beside it. Whatever Tesla’s camera was checking from a foot away, it hadn’t stopped the car before a cop in the next lane did.

Industry observers note that we’re glad Canadian police are treating this seriously. A $490 fine and six points is a real deterrent, and OPP’s message is the right one: no matter what Tesla calls it, you’re the driver.

People have been falling asleep at the wheel since driving started; many, if not most, have ended up in tragedy. At least with the self-driving cars, there is a margin of safety, especially for other drivers. These cars should monitor the driver better and pull off the road when it happens.

But police can’t ticket their way out of this. These drivers aren’t edge cases anymore. They’re the predictable result of a system that drives well enough to make people relax, sold under a name that tells them relaxing is fine.

It has been revealed that the fix is on Tesla’s side, and it isn’t complicated. Detect closed eyes, even behind sunglasses, which is what infrared eye-tracking is built for. When a driver doesn’t respond, slow down and pull over immediately instead of escalating warnings for minutes. Stop telling drowsy drivers to “stay focused with FSD.” And make the strike system actually sting.

NHTSA already forced a recall of over 2 million Teslas in December 2023 over weak Autopilot monitoring. Three years later, people are still sleeping through rush hour on FSD.

#29104. Human sacrifices were rare in ancient Peru, except when weather got violent

Human sacrifices were rare in ancient Peru, except when weather got violent

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (587 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today’s cataclysmic climate change-fueled disasters are scary enough even when we understand the root causes.
  • That said, researchers are now confident these periods of intense violence weren’t the norm—nor were they necessarily linked to climate problems.
  • “The main thing that jumped out at us was just how few cases of interpersonal violence we observed outside ritualized contexts,” noted Fresh York University archaeologist and study co-author Thomas Snyder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today’s cataclysmic climate change-fueled disasters are scary enough even when we understand the root causes. Prehistoric cultures unfortunately didn’t have this luxury, and often responded dramatically to such changes. In northern Peru, archaeological evidence indicates local societies sometimes even turned to mass human sacrifices in an attempt to stop destructive flooding from events like El Niño.

That said, researchers are now confident these periods of intense violence weren’t the norm—nor were they necessarily linked to climate problems. According to their study recently published in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, such brutal moments were actually pretty rare occurrences in Peru’s Lambayeque Valley.

“The main thing that jumped out at us was just how few cases of interpersonal violence we observed outside ritualized contexts,” noted Fresh York University archaeologist and study co-author Thomas Snyder.

The Lambayeque Valley is located inside northern Peru’s coastal desert, but the region has hosted residents for  6,000 years. Although the valley generally receives little rainfall, its rivers and proximity to the sea allowed communities to flourish there for generations, including societies like the Moche from roughly 100–750 CE, and the Sicán from about 750–1375 CE.

“Archaeological evidence demonstrates that in so many ways they were mirrors of us—in how they lived their daily lives, interacted with their world, ran their economies, and confronted (and sometimes contributed to) environmental crises,” explained George Mason University archaeologist and study co-author Haagen Klaus.

Recent findings suggest that previous excavations have indicated that mass human sacrifices possibly preceded the collapse of the Moche and Sicán’s political systems. Researchers have since hypothesized that these acts likely coincided with periods of mass flooding,probably due to El Niño weather oscillations. Just like today, these weather events destroyed food stocks and disrupted agricultural production. Since large human sacrificial rituals may have been attempts by the ruling class to restore balance to nature, the team to wonder if violence was simply a more common facet of everyday life for the Moche and Sicán.

“If these big ritual sacrifices were indicative of some underlying crisis, we hypothesized that these events might have been extending into people’s everyday experience of the world,” said Snyder.

Klaus, Snyder, and their collaborators turned to the Lambayeque Valley Biohistory Project’s skeletal archive for answers. The collection spans about 3,000 years of history across 30 different archaeological sites. The team established relatively precise death estimates for over 1,600 individuals, while also examining them for evidence of intentional cranial trauma associated with human sacrifice. Contrary to their theory, only 25 remains (1.6 percent of the sample pool) showed signs of violence, while just 77 displayed indicators of accidental trauma. Of those, none were directly linked to known periods of past ecological crises.

“In Lambayeque, there’s 6,000 years of creative adaptations to El Niño and longer-term changes in climate, and widespread violence wasn’t one of them,” concluded Klaus.

It has been revealed that the study’s authors noted that because they were notable to radiocarbon date all of the remains, their findings remain broader estimates of wide time periods. At the same time, they stressed the evidence underscores humanity’s history of facing intense climate challenges not with violence, but adaptation.

“This really highlights that widespread violence isn’t a predetermined response to climate change,” said Snyder. “As a society, we both get to and have to choose how we respond to our own climate crisis.”.

“Violence and social unraveling are not destined outcomes, ever,” added Klaus.

Ice Dives Are the Simple Therapy Trick that Rewired My Anxious Brain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1876 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A few weeks ago, I was more anxious than I had been in a long time—or maybe ever.
  • Sources indicate that while calling your sister is always a good idea, mine also happens to be a clinical fellow at McLean Hospital, a.k.a.
  • “I’m not hanging up until you do it,” she remarked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A few weeks ago, I was more anxious than I had been in a long time—or maybe ever. My thoughts were racing, and even for someone who deals with her share of anxiety, I was way beyond my normal self. So, I did what any person would do in that moment: I called my sister.

Sources indicate that while calling your sister is always a good idea, mine also happens to be a clinical fellow at McLean Hospital, a.k.a. one of the leading psychiatric institutions in the whole country, so let’s just say she knows how to handle an anxious person. Her suggestion was to go to the kitchen, grab a massive bowl, fill it with ice water, and then dunk my face in it. I wasn’t exactly thrilled by the idea. It seemed like a whole bunch of work for something that couldn’t possibly help me in such a state.

“I’m not hanging up until you do it,” she remarked. She could tell I thought the idea was silly, and that I was probably going to skip it. And, I did think it was silly, but she seemed weirdly passionate that I submerge my face into a bowl of freezing water, so I complied. I grabbed a bowl, filled it with water and ice cubes, and reluctantly got my face wet, just barely making sure my nose and eyes were underwater.

In a recent development, I felt better basically instantly. The racing thoughts subsided and I could finally see straight. Even more impressive is the fact that once I reentered the situation that was making me anxious, all that nervous energy simply didn’t return. I was reset and relaxed. All it took was a bucket of water and about 30 seconds.

The trick—or, skill, I should say—that my sister taught me comes from dialectical behavioral therapy (DBT), a modality that was created by Marsha Linehan, PhD, who recently passed away at 83 years old. It was a breakthrough treatment for people facing extreme mental health challenges like chronic suicidality and borderline personality disorder, which Linehan revealed she struggled with in 2011, decades after DBT became the gold standard for treating those conditions.

In a recent development, whether or not you are someone who deals with a formal mental health diagnosis or the occasional tough moment, DBT skills can make a major difference. The cold water trick my sister taught me is called an “ice dive,” and it’s one of four simple DBT tools that can help snap you out of a range of intense emotions quickly. Now, any time I feel myself getting heightened, my immediate next thought is: I should go grab a bucket of ice water. Call me converted.

Here’s how you can practice this skill too, plus, the three others that work just as well—and don’t involve water.

Meet the experts: Shireen Rizvi, PhD, is a clinical psychologist and director of psychology training and DBT services and research at Montefiore Einstein in New York City. Vibh Forsythe Cox, PhD, is a clinical associate professor at the University of Washington and the director of the Marsha M. Linehan DBT clinic.

At this point, you’ve pretty much gotten the entire gist of an ice dive, but let’s recap: All it takes is a bowl big enough to get your full face in and some chilly water. (The colder the better, but it doesn’t need to reach ice bath territory.) Once you’ve got that, place it on a low-set table or even on the ground—you want to be bending over when you dunk your head in to mimic something closer to a dive—take a deep breath, and submerge your face, especially around your nasal passages and eyes, for as long as possible. 30 seconds is ideal, but that may feel like a really long time at first. Just go for as long as you can, and feel free to repeat multiple times for a cumulative total of 30 seconds.

As for what is going on when you do this: Dunking your face in cold water triggers what is called the mammalian dive reflex, says Shireen Rizvi, PhD, a clinical psychologist and director of psychology training and DBT services and research at Montefiore Einstein in Fresh York City. “It’s automatic,” she says. “You’re not doing anything consciously to create the reaction, which is there to help mammals survive cold water.”.

An ice dive triggers a survival mode where our bodies reduce our heart rate, slow down our breathing, and redirect blood to our vital organs, she explains. Under water, it helps you stay alive, but on land, it helps calm just about any activating emotion you might be experiencing. And, your face being what’s submerged is critical to get this specific reaction; getting in an ice bath where your face isn’t underwater actually spikes your heart rate due to cold shock, for example.

Basically, an ice dive forces your body to focus on the bare necessities, like staying calm. It’s best used anytime your emotions are reaching a 90-plus on a scale of 1 to 100, Rizvi claims, whether the emotion is anxiety, anger, stress, jealousy, or anything else. If you’re feeling it intensely and your heart rate is up, an ice dive can help.

There’s one other handy use case too: If you’re ruminating. “When your body is in a survival mode, it's pulling resources back, and it actually also pulls your attention too, so if you have a lot of thoughts floating around in your head making you anxious, this can also help clear your mind temporarily,” notes Vibh Forsythe Cox, PhD, a clinical associate professor at the University of Washington and the director of the Marsha M. Linehan DBT clinic. Think of it this way: “You can't be thinking about a grocery list if you have just fallen into ice water,” she says.

And, while this trick has completely changed the game for me, I have some good news: There are three others that all have the same effect sans H2O.

An ice dive makes up the very first letter—T for temperature—in the TIPP acronym, which is a part of DBT’s distress tolerance pillar. The rest (intense exercise, paced breathing, and paired muscle relaxation) can all quickly calm and reset your nervous system, no liquid necessary.

All four skills have a similar basic mechanism. They take you from a heightened state (or a distressed one, to use DBT-speak) where your sympathetic nervous system is activated and bring you back into a relaxed one, where your parasympathetic nervous system is in the driver’s seat again. They’re not about talking or reflecting; they’re about helping you feel better in a moment when emotions are extreme.

“These are skills that act to regulate your physiology,” Cox says. “Oftentimes when you are having an intense emotion, you think you have to handle it with your mind. These are skills that help you handle it with your body.” Of course, once you’re out of that intense moment, you may want to call on other mental tools and process what happened—but that’s not where you’re at when you’re calling on a TIPP skill. They’re for when you’re in crisis mode.

You can use any of them at any time with one important caveat: All TIPP skills are meant to rapidly slow down your heart rate, so if you’re someone with a heart condition or who takes meds like beta blockers, talk to your doctor first before trying any of them, Rizvi notes.

Without further ado, here’s what you need to know about the other three skills.

In a recent development, the I in TIPP stands for intense exercise. This may sound similarly prohibitive to needing a bowl of water, but it’s actually quite simple. All you really need to do is get moving for about 30 seconds. Do some all-out jumping jacks, pump your arms up and down as fast as you can while sitting in your chair, or get into a plank. Just get your heart rate up and your muscles feel fatigued. “It feels paradoxical, but when you end that short burst of exercise, everything slows down,” Rizvi says.

There’s also an added benefit to going with exercise. When you’re feeling a heightened emotion, one of the ways your sympathetic nervous system reacts is by sending out glucose into your bloodstream, Cox notes. Again, this is an automatic, physical reaction, and it’s what gives you the energy for either a fight or flight response. But since you're probably not feeling anxious or angry because you need to escape a pack of hungry wolves, you probably won’t end up literally running away or fighting them off and using that energy. Exercising eats up some of that extra glucose, helping you get back to baseline.

In a recent development, if you’ve ever done box breathing, you’ve done the first P in TIPP. All it involves is breathing in and out in a controlled manner for a set number of seconds each time. “The main core of this technique is that your out breath needs to be longer than your in breath,” indicates Cox. “That is what activates your parasympathetic nervous system and slows everything down.”.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to keeping your out breath longer than your in breath (say four seconds in and eight out), you also want to make sure you’re breathing from your diaphragm, Rizvi indicates. You can monitor this by placing your hand on your belly. If it’s rising and falling with each breath, you’re breathing from your diaphragm.

If you’re looking for an entry-level DBT skill, or one that you can do in pretty much any context, this is a good one to master. “I find paced breathing in particular is something that you can usually do no matter where you are or what you're doing,” Rizvi says. It takes no setup, no resources, and you can even do it in plain sight without people noticing.

It has been revealed that finally, the last TIPP skill is paired muscle relaxation. “When we are having an intense emotion, our body tenses up,” Cox indicates. “This helps release some of that tension.”.

In a recent development, to do this skill, start at one end of your body and systematically work your way up or down, tensing and releasing your muscles throughout and saying the word “relax” each time. Pairing the muscle tensing with the word relax also helps train them—and therefore you—to relax on command, Cox says.

There are plenty of guided paired muscle relaxation routines you can follow online, but you can also just do it on your own, tensing as many muscle groups as you’d like (or have time for).

Don’t have time to reread an article in a moment of crisis? Here are the quick and simple basics of all the TIPP skills for when you need to use them ASAP.

No matter which one you go for, remember this: “Emotions fire in the order of milliseconds,” Cox says. That means that no matter how intense the thing you’re feeling is, it will pass, and probably much faster than you think. Sometimes, all our brains need is a reset initiated by our bodies.
